title: Myeloid Flow Patterns: APL, t(8;21), MDS and PNH
summary: Learn the flow cytometry signatures of acute promyelocytic leukaemia and AML with t(8;21), why myelodysplasia needs several combined aberrancies, and how PNH is detected by GPI-anchor loss in at least two lineages using FLAER on white cells.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 35 Hit 7 (APL and t(8;21) immunophenotypes), Hit 9 (PNH by GPI-anchored protein loss with FLAER; two lineages; WBC clones larger), Hit 10 (MDS flow pattern; combined abnormalities) and Exam Trap 6 (single MDS-type abnormality). Checked against Ally 2024, Kankhaw 2025, Xu 2014, Gupta 2021, Wang 2021, Bento 2017, Porwit 2023 (ELN/iMDSFlow), Lima 2020 and Brando 2019, all read via Europe PMC full text. Sources show the APL phenotype is suggestive, not diagnostic (NPM1-mutated AML can be APL-like; the microgranular variant often expresses CD34; PML::RARA confirms) (register flag rv-ch35-apl-phenotype-suggestive). The reviewer lists CD55 and CD59 with the WBC reagents and implies FLAER for all lineages; Lima 2020 states FLAER is used only on white cells and CD55/CD59 are not recommended for WBC analysis, with CD59 used for red cells (register flag rv-ch35-pnh-flaer-wbc-only). The reviewer’s “dim CD19” for t(8;21) is not taught as an intensity (sources read describe aberrant CD19 without specifying dim). Not taught: the Number Vault PNH example clone sizes, MRD, CD4 counts.

objectives: Describe the typical flow phenotypes of acute promyelocytic leukaemia and of AML with t(8;21), and state why APL needs genetic confirmation.
List common MDS-associated flow aberrancies and explain why no single aberrancy is diagnostic.
Describe how PNH is detected by flow, including FLAER on white cells, CD59 on red cells and the two-lineage rule.

scenes.title: Enough to call it?
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three flow cytometry requests — (1) an adult with bleeding and DIC labs whose marrow cells have high side scatter, bright CD33, and lack CD34 and HLA-DR; (2) a cytopenic adult whose only flow finding is CD7 on a small fraction of CD34-positive cells; (3) a young adult with dark urine, recently transfused, whose red cells show a small CD59-negative population. Question token: “Is one pattern enough to call it?”

cues.text: Three flow requests. First: an adult with bleeding and coagulation failure; the marrow cells are granular, bright for CD33, and lack CD34 and HLA-DR.
Second: a cytopenic adult whose only finding is CD7 on a few CD34-positive cells. Third: a recently transfused patient with dark urine and a small CD59-negative red-cell population.
In each case, is one flow pattern enough to make the diagnosis?

scenes.title: Normal maturation and the GPI anchor
scenes.altText: Schematic cards. Normal myeloid maturation: as cells mature toward promyelocytes they lose CD34 and decrease CD45 and HLA-DR, increase CD13, CD33, CD38 and CD117, and start to gain CD15 and CD64. Normal neutrophils are granular: their side scatter (SSC) is judged against lymphocytes as an internal standard. GPI anchor card: many blood-cell proteins hang on a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor, including the complement regulators CD55 and CD59; FLAER, a fluorescent inactive aerolysin, binds the GPI anchor itself on white cells.

cues.text: Start with normal marrow. As myeloid cells mature toward promyelocytes, they lose CD34 and lower HLA-DR, increase CD13, CD33 and CD117, and start to gain CD15 and CD64.
Normal neutrophils are full of granules, so their side scatter is high. Laboratories judge it against lymphocytes, which act as an internal standard.
Many blood-cell proteins hang on a GPI anchor, including CD55 and CD59, which protect the cell from complement.
FLAER, a fluorescent, inactive form of the toxin aerolysin, binds the GPI anchor itself on white cells, so a cell without anchors stays dark.

scenes.title: Leukaemia signatures: APL and t(8;21)
scenes.altText: APL card: abnormal promyelocytes with high SSC, strong myeloperoxidase, bright CD33, heterogeneous CD13 and CD117, and low or absent CD34, HLA-DR and CD11b. Microgranular variant: lower SSC, more often CD2 and CD34 positive. Confirmation card: diagnosis rests on the PML::RARA fusion from t(15;17), shown by FISH or RT-PCR; NPM1-mutated AML can show an APL-like CD34−/HLA-DR− phenotype. t(8;21) card: AML with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 shows high CD34 on blasts with aberrant B-cell markers (CD19, PAX5, cytoplasmic CD79a) and, in a subset, CD56; CD19 positivity was linked with lower relapse risk in one cohort.

cues.text: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia, APL, has a classic pattern: granular cells with high side scatter, strong myeloperoxidase and bright CD33, with CD34, HLA-DR and CD11b low or absent.

The microgranular variant has lower side scatter and more often expresses CD2 and CD34. The pattern suggests APL; the diagnosis rests on finding the PML::RARA fusion, from the 15;17 translocation, by FISH or RT-PCR.
Why not trust the phenotype alone? A subset of NPM1-mutated AML also lacks CD34 and HLA-DR, an APL-like look-alike.
AML with the 8;21 translocation, RUNX1::RUNX1T1, shows a different signature: high CD34 on blasts, with borrowed B-cell markers such as CD19, PAX5 or cytoplasmic CD79a, and CD56 in a subset of cases.

scenes.title: Marrow-failure patterns: MDS and PNH
scenes.altText: MDS card: aberrancies include reduced granulocyte SSC (granulocyte-to-lymphocyte SSC ratio), abnormal CD13/CD16 maturation pattern, and CD2, CD5, CD7 or CD56 on CD34-positive cells; the ELN/iMDSFlow group does not recommend using any single granulocytic marker in isolation; scores combine several parameters (Ogata score, cut-off ≥2). PNH card: red cells gated on CD235a and tested with CD59 (types I, II, III); neutrophils with FLAER plus CD24 and monocytes with FLAER plus CD14 (CD157 an alternative); at least two lineages; RBC clones are often smaller because PNH red cells are destroyed and transfused cells dilute them; high-sensitivity assays (0.01%) for aplastic anaemia and MDS. Hook answers card.

cues.text: In myelodysplasia, flow looks for many small clues: low granulocyte side scatter, an abnormal CD13 and CD16 maturation pattern, and CD2, CD5, CD7 or CD56 on CD34-positive cells.
No single clue counts on its own. The European working group advises against using any single granulocyte marker in isolation, and scores such as the Ogata score combine several.

For PNH, red cells are tested with CD59, while neutrophils are tested with FLAER plus CD24, and monocytes with FLAER plus CD14. At least two lineages are studied, and the red-cell clone is often smaller, because PNH red cells are destroyed and transfused cells dilute them.
Back to the hook. Case one needs urgent PML::RARA testing. Case two is not enough for MDS. Case three needs FLAER-based white-cell testing, which shows the clone better than red cells.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “CD34−/HLA-DR− = APL” (✓ suggestive only; NPM1-mutated AML can mimic it; confirm PML::RARA); “One MDS-type abnormality = MDS” (✓ combine findings; a small population of normal precursors can express CD7, and abnormal CD56 on monocytes can also occur in recovering marrow or infection); “The red-cell clone size is the PNH clone size” (✓ red cells underestimate it after hemolysis and transfusion; study white cells with FLAER).

cues.text: Trap one: lack of CD34 and HLA-DR proves APL. No: it is suggestive, NPM1-mutated AML can look the same, and PML::RARA confirms.

Trap two: one MDS-type abnormality means MDS. No: a small population of normal precursors can express CD7, and abnormal CD56 on monocytes can also occur in recovering marrow or infection. Combine findings.
Trap three: the red-cell result shows the true PNH clone size. No: hemolysis and transfusion shrink it, so white cells are studied with FLAER.

props.title: ✗ “One MDS-type clue = MDS.”
lines: ✓ CD7 can occur on normal precursors; combine clues

scenes.title: Hide, borrow, pile, drop
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “APL HIDES its youth badges (no CD34, no HLA-DR) but shouts CD33; t(8;21) BORROWS a B-cell badge (CD19); MDS needs a PILE of small clues; PNH cells DROP the anchor that holds their badges, so FLAER finds nothing to grab.” Tokens: hide = APL · borrow = t(8;21) · pile = MDS · drop = PNH. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: hide, borrow, pile, drop. APL hides its youth badges, CD34 and HLA-DR. The 8;21 leukaemia borrows a B-cell badge, CD19. MDS needs a pile of clues. PNH cells drop the anchor, so FLAER has nothing to grab.

Where it breaks: other leukaemias also hide CD34 and HLA-DR, and the microgranular variant of APL often expresses CD34, so genetics decides; FLAER is used on white cells, not red cells; and several different MDS scores exist.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: FLAER is for white cells, not red cells

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “APL-like phenotype → confirm PML::RARA · t(8;21) = high CD34 with CD19”, “MDS = several combined clues · PNH = FLAER on white cells, at least two lineages”.

cues.text: Treat myeloid flow patterns as clues rather than verdicts: an APL-like phenotype needs PML::RARA confirmation, MDS needs several combined aberrancies, and PNH needs GPI-anchor loss shown in at least two lineages, with FLAER on white cells.

props.label: APL-like → confirm PML::RARA · t(8;21) = CD34 high + CD19
MDS = combined clues · PNH = FLAER on WBC, ≥ 2 lineages

explanation.what: Plain language: flow cytometry reads the “badges” on blood cells. Some leukaemias have recognisable badge patterns, but look-alikes exist, so genetics confirms. In myelodysplasia, many small badge errors together point to disease, never one alone. In PNH, cells lose the anchor that holds several badges, and a fluorescent toxin that binds the anchor shows which white cells lack it. Scientific terms: acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL), PML::RARA, t(15;17), microgranular variant, NPM1-mutated AML, RUNX1::RUNX1T1, t(8;21), CD19, PAX5, cytoplasmic CD79a, CD56, side scatter (SSC), CD13/CD16 maturation pattern, cross-lineage antigen, Ogata score, glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor, CD55, CD59, FLAER (fluorescent aerolysin), CD24, CD14, CD157, CD235a, type I/II/III red cells, high-sensitivity assay.
explanation.why: APL is linked with life-threatening coagulopathy and needs prompt recognition, but its phenotype overlaps with other AML, so a suspicious pattern triggers urgent genetic testing. MDS aberrancies also occur in other conditions, so combining several reduces false calls. PNH red cells are destroyed by complement and diluted by transfusion, so white-cell testing gives a better estimate of the clone.
explanation.measure: APL: high SSC, strong MPO, bright CD33, heterogeneous CD13/CD117, low or absent CD34, HLA-DR and CD11b; microgranular variant: lower SSC, more CD2/CD34; confirm PML::RARA by FISH or RT-PCR. t(8;21): high CD34 on blasts, CD19/PAX5/cCD79a and CD56. MDS: reduced granulocyte SSC (compared with lymphocytes), abnormal CD13/CD16 pattern, CD2/CD5/CD7/CD56 on CD34+ cells; no single granulocytic marker in isolation; scores combine parameters (Ogata ≥2). PNH: RBC gated on CD235a and tested with CD59; neutrophils FLAER + CD24, monocytes FLAER + CD14 (CD157 alternative); at least two lineages; high-sensitivity (0.01%) assays for aplastic anaemia and MDS.
explanation.differs: APL (CD34−/HLA-DR−, high SSC, PML::RARA) vs NPM1-mutated APL-like AML (some HLA-DR/CD15, monocytes, lower SSC); APL vs t(8;21) AML (high CD34 with B-cell markers); single aberrancy vs combined aberrancies; FLAER (white cells) vs CD59 (red cells); red-cell clone (underestimated) vs white-cell clone.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: recognise the APL phenotype and pick genetic confirmation, recognise the t(8;21) B-marker pattern, reject an MDS call based on one finding, or choose the correct PNH reagents and lineages.

mnemonic.text: Hide, borrow, pile, drop: APL HIDES its youth badges (no CD34, no HLA-DR) but shouts CD33; t(8;21) BORROWS a B-cell badge (CD19); MDS needs a PILE of small clues; PNH cells DROP the anchor, so FLAER has nothing to grab.
mnemonic.explanation: One verb per pattern links each disease to its key flow finding.
mnemonic.limitation: Other AML (such as NPM1-mutated AML) can also lack CD34 and HLA-DR, and the microgranular APL variant often expresses CD34, so genetics decides; FLAER is used on white cells, not red cells; several different MDS scoring systems exist.

analogyLimitations: Flow plots are shown as schematic cards, not real cytometry data.
Marker patterns are typical, not universal; individual cases vary.
takeaway: Treat myeloid flow patterns as clues rather than verdicts: an APL-like phenotype needs PML::RARA confirmation, MDS needs several combined aberrancies, and PNH needs GPI-anchor loss shown in at least two lineages, with FLAER on white cells.

questions.stem: An adult with bleeding and DIC laboratory findings has marrow cells with high side scatter, strong myeloperoxidase, bright CD33, heterogeneous CD117, and no CD34, HLA-DR or CD11b. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Suggestive of APL; confirm urgently by testing for PML::RARA (FISH or RT-PCR)
options.rationale: Correct. This is the classic APL pattern, but other AML can look similar, and the diagnosis rests on the PML::RARA fusion.

options.text: Diagnostic of APL; genetic testing is unnecessary
options.rationale: Incorrect. NPM1-mutated AML can show an APL-like CD34−/HLA-DR− phenotype, so the fusion must be shown.
Incorrect. AML with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 usually has high CD34 on blasts with B-cell markers such as CD19.

options.text: APL is excluded because CD117 is expressed
options.rationale: Incorrect. CD117 is often expressed, heterogeneously, in APL.

questions.stem: A cytopenic adult’s marrow shows a small CD7-positive subset of CD34-positive cells; all other flow parameters are normal. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Not sufficient for an MDS flow interpretation; MDS-related aberrancies are combined, not used in isolation
options.rationale: Correct. MDS flow interpretation needs several combined aberrancies, and a small population of normal precursors can express CD7, especially in recovering marrow.
Incorrect. One aberrancy is never enough; MDS diagnosis integrates combined flow findings with morphology and cytogenetics.
Incorrect. A small CD7-positive subset of CD34-positive cells can occur in normal or recovering marrow; nothing else here suggests a T-lymphoblast population.

options.text: CD7 is never found on normal myeloid precursors, so the sample is abnormal
options.rationale: Incorrect. A small population of normal precursors can express CD7, especially in recovering marrow, so its presence alone is not proof of abnormality.

questions.stem: A recently transfused patient with hemoglobinuria is tested for PNH. Which approach best follows current flow practice?

options.text: FLAER plus CD24 on neutrophils and FLAER plus CD14 on monocytes, with CD59 on red cells
options.rationale: Correct. Studying at least two lineages, with FLAER-based white-cell testing, avoids underestimating the clone when red cells are destroyed or transfused.
Incorrect. FLAER is used only on white cells; red cells carry glycophorin A, a non-GPI protein that weakly binds aerolysin.
Incorrect. One lineage is not enough, red cells underestimate the clone after transfusion, and CD59 stains red cells more brightly than CD55.

Incorrect. This complement-based hemolysis test preceded flow cytometry and gives false positives in other disorders, such as congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia type II; flow testing of GPI-anchored proteins is used where available.

claims.text: Normal myeloid maturation antigen changes; neutrophil SSC judged against lymphocytes.
APL phenotype (high SSC, strong MPO, bright CD33, heterogeneous CD13/CD117, low/absent CD34, HLA-DR, CD11b); microgranular variant lower SSC, more CD2/CD34; linked with DIC.
APL diagnosis rests on PML::RARA (t(15;17)) by FISH or RT-PCR; NPM1-mutated AML can be APL-like.
AML with RUNX1::RUNX1T1: high CD34, aberrant CD19, PAX5, cCD79a, CD56 in a subset; CD19 linked with lower relapse risk in one cohort.

MDS flow aberrancies (low granulocyte SSC, abnormal CD13/CD16 pattern, CD2/CD5/CD7/CD56 on CD34+ cells); no single granulocytic marker in isolation; scores combine parameters; CD7 on some normal precursors and monocyte CD56 outside MDS.

GPI-AP loss (CD55, CD59); FLAER binds GPI anchor and is used on WBC only; FLAER + CD24/CD14 (CD157 alternative); CD59 with CD235a gating on RBC; at least two lineages; RBC clone underestimated; high-sensitivity assays; Ham test false positives.
The reviewer’s “dim CD19” intensity in t(8;21) AML.
claims.note: Sources read describe aberrant CD19 expression but not its intensity; not taught as dim.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 35 Hit 7 presents HLA-DR−, CD34 low/absent, bright CD33 as the APL immunophenotype that correlates with t(15;17). Ally 2024, Gupta 2021 and Kankhaw 2025 show NPM1-mutated AML can be APL-like (CD34−/HLA-DR−), the microgranular variant often expresses CD34, and diagnosis rests on PML::RARA by FISH or RT-PCR; the lesson teaches the phenotype as suggestive only (register flag rv-ch35-apl-phenotype-suggestive).

Ch. 35 Hit 9 lists CD55 and CD59 with CD24, CD14 and CD157 and says PNH is diagnosed “using FLAER”. Lima 2020 states FLAER is used only on white cells (red cells weakly bind aerolysin via glycophorin A), CD59 with CD235a gating is used for red cells, and CD55/CD59 are not recommended for white-cell analysis; the lesson teaches reagents by lineage (register flag rv-ch35-pnh-flaer-wbc-only).

morphology.note: No cytometry plots or images; patterns described on schematic cards.

verification.notes: 6 factual claims checked against Ally 2024, Kankhaw 2025, Xu 2014, Gupta 2021, Wang 2021, Bento 2017, Porwit 2023, Lima 2020 and Brando 2019 (all Europe PMC full text); 1 pending (the reviewer’s “dim CD19” intensity in t(8;21), not taught).
